name: Uma Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for talking with me, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the personal tax team at a firm of about eighty people in the city centre. I cycle in, and most of my day is tax returns for landlords, freelancers and a surprising number of session musicians. I spend a lot of time chasing people for rental statements and working out which of their expenses actually count.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle when someone's affairs are a mess and I get them straight, and the relief in their voice when I tell them the bill. What wears me out is the chasing, and the same twenty questions every January. I use an AI tool now and then to draft the reminder emails, once a couple of colleagues showed me it was fine to.

S0.quote: My whole January used to be reminder emails, and now a tool writes them in my voice while I do the bits clients actually pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a handy helper for emails and not much else. At work I'd probably tell the manager we can stop worrying about it in the team meetings. I'm not really one for posting about work online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pleased. I'm good at the human side, talking a nervous landlord through a tax bill, and that would stay mine. Sami and I could keep saving for the flat on the plan we already have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and keep using the email drafting, because it saves me maybe an hour a week. I'd put the hour into the advanced tax exam I've been meaning to sit. And we'd keep putting four hundred a month into the deposit fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, really. Like the forecast said rain and it turned out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything already worrying you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents in the city, mainly. Sami's a maths teacher and his pay doesn't move much, so the deposit takes forever. But both our jobs feel solid, and we've got about four months saved outside the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that saved hour a week actually look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, Friday afternoons. My whole January used to be reminder emails, and now a tool writes them in my voice while I do the bits clients actually pay for.

say: I'd call AI a **handy helper** for emails and not much more.
I'd suggest we **stop worrying** about it in team meetings.
think: The **human side** of tax work, calming nervous landlords, would stay mine.
Sami and I could stick to our **deposit plan** for a flat.
do: Keep using AI to draft **reminder emails**, saving about an hour a week.
Use that hour to study for the **advanced tax** exam.
Keep putting **£400 a month** into the flat deposit.
feel: **Settled**, like a rainy forecast that turned out fine.
fieldNote: Uma's job and her partner's teaching job both feel **secure** to her.
She already uses AI in a **small, practical** way after colleagues proved it safe.
Her main pressure is **city rents**, which slow the deposit but don't threaten income.

steps.text: Keep drafting client reminder emails with the AI tool
Sit the advanced tax exam using the saved hour
Keep putting £400 a month into the flat deposit
Keep doing landlord and freelancer returns as now

S1.quote: I think the firm keeps the people who can explain a tax bill to a frightened client, and lets the box-fillers go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's much closer to home. Checking and answering customers is half my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say to a client: the firm is changing, but someone still has to sign the return and take the call. Among friends I'd admit it's a lot. I'd probably share an article or two, nothing angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the personal tax team is the obvious target. Pulling figures off a rental statement and filling in boxes is exactly what software is good at. I think the firm keeps the people who can explain a tax bill to a frightened client, and lets the box-fillers go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to go on the firm's AI course in the first month, once I'd seen it working for the team next door. I'd push to sit the advanced tax exam this year, because advice is harder to automate than forms. And we'd lift savings a bit, maybe another hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a useful way. Like the week before an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you think you'd land in that sort of cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Middle of the pack, which is the scary place. I'm not the star and I'm not the weakest. I'd need the qualification to move up a line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My manager, Grace, because she's straight with people. I'd ask her directly which roles she expects to keep in two years, and then plan around her answer.

say: I'd say **someone still signs** the return and takes the client's call.
I'd admit to friends it's a lot, and maybe **share an article**.
think: Personal tax box-filling is the **obvious target** for software.
The firm would keep **explainers** and cut **box-fillers**, and I'm mid-pack.
do: Sign up for the firm's **AI course** in the first month.
Sit the **advanced tax** exam this year to move towards advice.
feel: **Nervous** but focused, like the week before an exam.
fieldNote: Uma sees her **middle position** as the riskiest place in a cut.
Her plan is to **climb into advice**, which she thinks is harder to automate.
Waits to see a tool **proven** next door before joining, true to steady habits.

steps.text: Join the firm's AI course after seeing it work next door
Sit the advanced tax exam within the year
Add £100 a month to the household savings

S2.quote: My partner Sami and I would probably agree to stop saving for a flat and start saving to survive, and that's a sad conversation at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's two Januaries away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it calmly, because clients would be scared and someone has to sound normal. To friends I'd say it's not just us, it's every desk job. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't think there'd be a personal tax team by 2029. If a machine can do any thinking work as well as me and cheaper, my qualification is a piece of paper. Being on a screen all day means there's no three-year robot gap for me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the deposit fund and turn it into a living fund, because buying a flat on one uncertain salary would be mad. I'd start looking in the first few months at jobs with people in the room, like practice management or client care at a hospital trust. And I'd talk to my parents about whether we could move back to my hometown, where rent is half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened, not exam nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami say to each other about the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Sami and I would probably agree to stop saving for a flat and start saving to survive, and that's a sad conversation at twenty-seven. He'd say teaching has longer, which might even be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said practice management. Isn't that thinking work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, it is. I suppose I'm grabbing at anything with a person in it. I don't have a good answer for two years.

say: I'd stay **calm in public** because clients would be scared.
I'd tell friends it hits **every desk job**, not just accountants.
think: The **personal tax team** probably wouldn't exist by 2029.
My job is all screen work, so there's **no robot gap** for me.
do: Turn the **flat deposit** into a living fund straight away.
Apply for **people-facing** roles like client care within months.
Ask her parents about moving to her **hometown**, where rent is half.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose** her job and admits she has **no plan**.
The **flat deposit** is the clearest casualty, and that's what upsets her most.
When challenged, she accepts her fallback is **also thinking work**.

steps.text: Pause the flat purchase and use the deposit as living money
Apply for client care roles at the local hospital trust
Move back to her hometown where rent is half
Ask her parents for a room while they resettle

S3.quote: A two-year retraining course costs more than everything I've saved since university, so it only works if Sami covers the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That gives me a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them. At work I'd be pushing the team to learn the tools properly. I wouldn't be one of the doom people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think for about three years my job would actually get busier, using the AI to do more returns each. Then by 2031 it goes. So the question is what I am at thirty-two, and it isn't a tax preparer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools daily from now so I'm the one who supervises them, and I'd finish the advanced tax exam. Then around year three I'd look at retraining for something with a person in it, maybe speech therapy, which my cousin does. We'd hold off on buying the flat until we know where we'd live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but with a plan. Like knowing the motorway's closed ahead and taking the next exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why speech therapy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Nadia loves it, and it's hands-on with children. If thinking AI comes first and robots later, a job with real people in a room might last longer. I'd have to check if I could afford the two years of study though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on four months of savings. A two-year retraining course costs more than everything I've saved since university, so it only works if Sami covers the rent.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so let's use them.
I'd push the team to **learn the tools** properly, not panic.
think: My job gets **busier** for about three years, then disappears by **2031**.
At thirty-two I won't be a **tax preparer**.
do: Use AI tools **daily** so she supervises them rather than competes.
Look at **speech therapy** retraining around year three.
Delay **buying a flat** until they know where they'd live.
feel: **Worried** but holding a **plan**, like taking an exit before a closure.
fieldNote: Five years turns her from **frightened to planning**.
She uses the **robot gap** logic to pick a people-facing, hands-on career.
**Money** is the real limit: retraining depends on **Sami covering rent**.

steps.text: Use the firm's AI tools daily on every tax return
Research speech therapy courses with cousin Nadia's help
Delay buying a flat until the job picture clears
Ask Sami to cover the rent during two years' study

S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd buy the flat, have a baby, and retrain in that order, instead of panicking all three at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a career-change decade, not a crisis. At work I'd be open about planning ahead. With friends we'd probably joke about all becoming nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it still ends with me not doing tax. But ten years is long enough to finish one career properly and start another. With ten years' warning I'd buy the flat, have a baby, and retrain in that order, instead of panicking all three at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going in tax for the next four or five years, using AI more each year. We'd buy the flat in about two years while we both have steady pay. Then I'd start part-time study for a people-facing job around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy the flat. Isn't a mortgage risky if your job ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But if we buy somewhere modest while two salaries cover it, it's safer than renting forever. I'd only buy if the payment fits on Sami's pay alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the firm stops hiring graduates. If the trainee intake halves, I'd bring everything forward a couple of years.

say: I'd call it a **career-change decade**, not a crisis.
I'd be **open at work** about planning ahead, and joke with friends about all becoming nurses.
think: It still ends with me **not doing tax**, just more slowly.
Ten years lets me **finish one career** and start another properly.
do: Keep working in tax for **four or five years**, using AI more.
Buy a **modest flat** in about two years, affordable on Sami's pay.
Start **part-time study** for a people-facing job around 2031.
feel: Still **worried**, but able to see a **path**.
fieldNote: She still expects her **tax job to end**, so the mood stays anxious.
Ten years lets her **sequence** life events: flat, baby, retraining.
Sets a clear **trigger**: graduate intake halving brings plans forward.

steps.text: Keep preparing tax returns at the firm for five years
Take on more AI-assisted work each year
Buy a modest flat that Sami's pay alone covers
Start part-time study for a people-facing career around 2031

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I've planned, the flat and the exams, would be pointless overnight. What would help is help paying for a second degree, like a loan for career changers in their late twenties and thirties, because nobody can afford that on four months of savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much of this job is calming people down. A tax return is maths, but the phone call about the tax bill is a person who can't sleep, and I don't know who does that call after 2028.

headlineQuote: A tax return is maths, but the phone call about the tax bill is a person who can't sleep, and I don't know who does that call after 2028.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old accountant** on a city firm's personal tax team, serving landlords and freelancers.
She lives with Sami, a **maths teacher**, and they're saving for a **flat deposit**.
She uses AI for **reminder emails** and adopts tools once colleagues prove them.
Mild change suits her, but **two-year AGI** would wreck her plans and leave her frightened.
With more time she'd **sequence** a flat, a baby and a move into **people-facing** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would make her flat and exams **pointless**.
whatWouldHelp: A **study loan** for career changers in their late twenties and thirties.
